title: Recall bank, Q320–403
des: Oman Pearson VUE paediatrics recall bank, questions 320–403, with the answers explained in the tutor's audio review (May 2025). Answers checked and explained.

questions.question: A 6-year-old has a skin rash and a painful, tender, swollen right knee. There is no history of travel or animal contact. Blood tests show leucocytosis and a low C4. Which investigations should be done?
questions.exp: A low complement (C3/C4) with rash and arthritis raises the question of systemic lupus erythematosus, so check ANA and anti-dsDNA. A hot swollen joint with leucocytosis must also be investigated for infection (blood culture, and joint aspiration). Brucella testing is guided by animal contact or unpasteurised milk, which is absent here.

questions.question: A 13-year-old has asplenia. Which vaccines should he receive?
questions.c: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) followed by the polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23)
questions.exp: Without a spleen, children are at risk of overwhelming infection from encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis). They need pneumococcal conjugate then polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23 at least 8 weeks later, repeated after 5 years), Hib, meningococcal ACWY and B, and yearly influenza vaccine, plus daily penicillin prophylaxis and a fever plan.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl is seen for follow-up. Viral screening is negative. Her liver enzymes were slightly raised at the last visit, and now ALT is 100 and AST 72. She has iron deficiency; everything else is normal. What should be done?
questions.c: Repeat the liver function tests in 3 months
questions.exp: Mildly raised transaminases in a well child are first re-checked over time; liver biopsy is considered only if they stay raised for more than about 6 months without a cause. Meanwhile look for common causes: coeliac disease (anti-tTG, especially with iron deficiency), fatty liver, Wilson disease (over 3 years), autoimmune hepatitis, muscle disease (CK) and drugs.

questions.question: A newborn has a purpuric rash, intrauterine growth restriction, thrombocytopenia and raised liver enzymes from congenital cytomegalovirus infection. Which finding is typical on brain imaging?
questions.exp: Congenital CMV: periventricular calcification, microcephaly, ventriculomegaly, sensorineural hearing loss (the most common long-term problem), chorioretinitis, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly. Congenital toxoplasmosis gives diffuse scattered calcification with hydrocephalus. Treat symptomatic congenital CMV with valganciclovir for 6 months.

questions.question: A patient from Bangladesh has bloody diarrhoea, tenesmus and a feeling of incomplete defecation. Which organism is most likely?
questions.exp: Amoebic dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica) causes bloody diarrhoea with mucus and tenesmus in travellers from or residents of South Asia; it can cause liver abscess. Diagnose by stool microscopy, antigen or PCR; treat with metronidazole followed by a luminal agent (paromomycin). Enterotoxigenic E. coli, cholera, rotavirus and giardia cause watery, non-bloody diarrhoea. Shigella and Campylobacter are the other main causes of dysentery.

questions.question: A child is put on mechanical ventilation after a cardiac operation. What is the main benefit of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP)?
questions.a: It removes carbon dioxide by increasing tidal volume
questions.b: It keeps alveoli open and prevents alveolar collapse, improving oxygenation
questions.c: It increases venous return to the heart
questions.e: It reduces the need for sedation
questions.exp: PEEP keeps alveoli open at the end of expiration, recruits collapsed lung, increases functional residual capacity and improves oxygenation (with FiO2 and mean airway pressure). Too much PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return and cardiac output, and risks air leak. CO2 removal depends on minute ventilation (tidal volume x rate).

questions.question: A child with acute severe asthma has had nebulised salbutamol and IV hydrocortisone without improvement. What is the next step?
questions.b: Intravenous theophylline as the first add-on
questions.exp: Add nebulised ipratropium early, then give IV magnesium sulphate 40 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes if there is no response. IV salbutamol and aminophylline come after that, with intensive care review. Aminophylline has more side effects and is not the first add-on.

questions.question: A 3-day-old baby has a heavy purulent eye discharge with swollen eyelids. What is the management?
questions.e: A single dose of intramuscular ceftriaxone
questions.exp: Purulent conjunctivitis in the first 2–5 days is gonococcal until proven otherwise. Take swabs (Gram stain, culture, NAAT for gonorrhoea and chlamydia) and give one dose of ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg IM or IV (max 125 mg), with frequent saline irrigation. Treat the mother and partner.

questions.question: A neonate has a purulent eye discharge. The Gram stain shows Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the organism?
questions.exp: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci = Neisseria (gonorrhoeae in the eye or genital tract; meningitidis in CSF or blood). Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular organism not seen on Gram stain. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive diplococcus, and Haemophilus a Gram-negative coccobacillus.

questions.question: A floppy newborn has upslanting eyes, a high forehead with a large fontanelle, liver dysfunction and renal cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Zellweger syndrome is a peroxisomal biogenesis disorder (PEX genes, autosomal recessive): severe hypotonia, seizures, flat face with high forehead, large fontanelle and upslanting eyes, hepatomegaly with liver dysfunction, renal cortical cysts and stippled patellar calcification. Very long-chain fatty acids are raised. Most die in the first year.

questions.question: A boy has eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets and recurrent infections (Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome). What is the mode of inheritance?
questions.exp: Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (WAS gene, Xp11) affects boys: eczema, thrombocytopenia with SMALL platelets (bleeding), recurrent bacterial and viral infections, and a raised risk of autoimmunity and lymphoma. Cure is by stem cell transplant.

questions.question: A parent has an inherited disease that is passed to 50% of his children, whatever the partner's genes. Which of these diseases fits?
questions.exp: A 50% risk to each child from one affected parent, regardless of the other parent, is autosomal dominant inheritance: NF1, tuberous sclerosis, Marfan, achondroplasia, Huntington. CF, Pompe, sickle cell and PKU are autosomal recessive (25% risk when both parents are carriers).

questions.question: A 2-year-old with Kawasaki disease has had fever for 8 days, an ESR of 100 and a haemoglobin of 7.8 g/dL. Which finding indicates a poor prognosis?
questions.b: Very high inflammatory markers with a low haemoglobin
questions.exp: Risk scores for coronary aneurysm and IVIG resistance (Harada, Kobayashi) include young age (under 1 year), male sex, prolonged fever (over 10 days before treatment), anaemia, high CRP/ESR, low albumin, low sodium, high ALT and high neutrophils with low platelets. The mucocutaneous features themselves do not predict outcome.

questions.question: A child has a scenario typical of dengue fever on day 2 of illness. Which investigation confirms it?
questions.exp: Early in dengue (days 1–5) the virus or its NS1 antigen is in the blood, so use RT-PCR or NS1 antigen. IgM rises after day 5. Also monitor the full blood count (falling platelets and rising haematocrit warn of plasma leakage).

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl has had 3 episodes in the last year of fever, abdominal pain with constipation, and arthritis, with leucocytosis. She is completely healthy between episodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Familial Mediterranean fever: recurrent self-limited attacks (1–3 days) of fever with serositis (peritonitis, pleuritis), arthritis or an erysipelas-like rash, high inflammatory markers during attacks, and complete health in between. Common in Arab, Turkish, Armenian and Jewish people. Colchicine prevents attacks and amyloidosis. Crohn's disease and SLE do not fully settle between episodes.

questions.question: What is capnography (an end-tidal CO2 detector) used for after intubation?
questions.c: Confirming that the endotracheal tube is in the trachea
questions.d: Measuring the depth of the tube
questions.exp: A sustained exhaled CO2 trace confirms tracheal (not oesophageal) placement and is the gold standard, with chest movement and auscultation. During CPR a very low ETCO2 can mean poor cardiac output, and a sudden rise suggests return of circulation. Capnography does not measure oxygenation (use pulse oximetry or blood gas) or tube depth (use a chest X-ray).

questions.question: A child has had rhinorrhoea and cough; after 2 days he deteriorates, with reduced air entry and dullness to percussion on the right. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Reduced air entry with dullness on percussion means consolidation with fluid. A parapneumonic effusion complicates bacterial pneumonia, most often Streptococcus pneumoniae (also Staphylococcus aureus and group A strep). Confirm with chest X-ray and ultrasound; large or infected effusions need drainage. A pneumothorax is hyper-resonant.

questions.question: A child with acute pancreatitis has vomiting and epigastric pain, and a serum lipase of 270 U/L. What should be done?
questions.b: Keep nil by mouth for 2 weeks
questions.d: Repeat the pancreatic enzymes every few hours to guide treatment
questions.exp: The mainstay of acute pancreatitis treatment is early aggressive IV fluids, good pain relief and early feeding (oral or nasogastric when tolerated). Enzyme levels do not reflect severity and need not be repeated. Antibiotics are only for infected necrosis or cholangitis; ERCP only for an obstructing stone with cholangitis.

questions.question: A patient has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with bluish discoloration around the umbilicus and in the flanks. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Epigastric pain radiating to the back is typical of pancreatitis. Periumbilical bruising (Cullen sign) and flank bruising (Grey Turner sign) show retroperitoneal bleeding in severe (haemorrhagic, necrotising) pancreatitis. Causes in children: trauma (bicycle handlebar), gallstones, drugs (valproate, asparaginase), infections (mumps) and genetic causes.

questions.question: A 3-month-old has had a watery eye with crusting on the eyelashes since early infancy. The eye is otherwise normal. What should be done?
questions.c: Probing of the tear duct now under general anaesthesia
questions.e: Teach the parents lacrimal sac massage
questions.exp: Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction causes constant tearing and sticky discharge; 90% resolve by 1 year. Management: massage over the lacrimal sac (Crigler massage) and cleaning, with topical antibiotics only for infection. Refer for probing if it persists after 12 months. Refer urgently if there is a red eye, cloudy or large cornea or photophobia (congenital glaucoma).

questions.question: A child has fever, a maculopapular rash, cough and conjunctivitis (measles). Which complication can appear years later?
questions.exp: SSPE is a rare, fatal, progressive brain disease 7–10 years after measles (mostly when infected under 2 years): behaviour change, myoclonus, dementia, with periodic complexes on EEG and high measles antibody in CSF. Early complications are otitis media, pneumonia (the main cause of death), diarrhoea, encephalitis, and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis 1–3 weeks later. Coronary aneurysm is Kawasaki disease.

questions.question: Which burn pattern is LEAST suggestive of non-accidental injury?
questions.a: A glove burn with a sharp line at the wrist
questions.b: Burns on both buttocks sparing the centre (doughnut pattern)
questions.d: A sock burn with a sharp line at the ankle
questions.e: An irregular burn on the chest with splash marks
questions.exp: Abusive immersion burns are symmetrical with sharp tide-lines (glove and stocking distribution, buttocks and perineum with a spared centre where the skin pressed on the bath). Cigarette burns are round, about 8 mm. Accidental spill burns are irregular, with an uneven depth and splash marks, often on the face, chest and arm as the child pulls a hot drink down.

questions.question: A 15-year-old girl has diarrhoea, swelling of both parotid glands and dental erosion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Repeated self-induced vomiting causes parotid swelling, dental enamel erosion, calluses on the knuckles (Russell sign) and hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; laxative misuse causes diarrhoea. Weight is often normal in bulimia nervosa. Treat with CBT for bulimia; correct electrolytes.

questions.question: A 2-month-old presents with poor feeding and a blood glucose of 2 mmol/L. Heart rate is 170/min and BP 90/50. Which tests should be sent at the time of hypoglycaemia?
questions.a: No tests; give glucose and discharge
questions.d: Bone profile, cortisol, insulin and thyroid function
questions.e: Cortisol, insulin, thyroid function and growth hormone (with ketones and other metabolites)
questions.exp: Take a "critical sample" during hypoglycaemia, before giving glucose: glucose, insulin, C-peptide, cortisol, growth hormone, beta-hydroxybutyrate, free fatty acids, lactate, ammonia, acylcarnitines, plus urine organic acids, and thyroid function. Low ketones with high insulin = hyperinsulinism; low cortisol/GH suggests hypopituitarism or adrenal insufficiency. PTH and the bone profile are not part of this work-up.

questions.question: A preterm baby born by vaginal delivery has respiratory distress (RR 72) with a good Apgar score and is breathing well. While waiting for the chest X-ray, what should be done?
questions.e: Observe in air with no support
questions.exp: A breathing preterm baby with respiratory distress should start on CPAP early; surfactant is given if oxygen needs rise despite CPAP. Take blood cultures and start antibiotics too, but antibiotics alone do not treat the breathing problem.

questions.question: A preterm baby of 35 weeks starts feeds and develops early high bilirubin within 52 hours. The direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test is positive. What is the cause of the jaundice?
questions.exp: Jaundice in the first 1–2 days with a positive direct Coombs test means immune haemolysis: ABO (mother O, baby A or B) or rhesus disease. Galactosaemia gives later jaundice with liver dysfunction, cataracts and E. coli sepsis after milk feeds; breast milk jaundice starts after the first week.

questions.question: A 25-day-old baby is in shock with cold peripheries, weak pulses in all four limbs and an unrecordable blood pressure. There is no response to 40 mL/kg of fluid. Antibiotics have been given. What is the next step?
questions.d: Give a further 60 mL/kg of fluid quickly
questions.e: Wait for the echocardiogram before any treatment
questions.exp: Fluid-refractory shock in an infant needs an inotrope (adrenaline for cold shock, or dopamine), through a peripheral or intraosseous line if needed, plus airway support. In a neonate, always think of a duct-dependent heart lesion (weak or absent femoral pulses, hepatomegaly, gallop): if suspected, start prostaglandin E1 without waiting for the echo.

questions.question: A baby is born in the labour room and is not breathing well after initial drying and stimulation. What is the first action?
questions.a: Positive pressure ventilation with a bag and mask
questions.exp: Newborn life support: dry, warm and stimulate; if not breathing or heart rate below 100, open the airway and give inflation breaths then ventilation breaths (bag-mask or T-piece). Ventilation is the most important step. Chest compressions start only if the heart rate stays below 60 despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation; drugs through an umbilical line come after that.

questions.question: A mother at 22 weeks of pregnancy is told her baby has a lethal skeletal dysplasia (severe rickets-like bone changes). When should perinatal palliative care be involved?
questions.b: Only when the family asks for it
questions.c: At the first admission to the neonatal unit
questions.exp: Palliative care should start as soon as a life-limiting diagnosis is made antenatally. It supports decisions about the birth plan, resuscitation and comfort care, and helps the family prepare. It runs alongside obstetric care and does not mean the end of other care.

questions.question: A child who has a cat at home has an enlarged, tender lymph node. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae, mostly from kittens): a papule at the scratch, then tender regional lymphadenopathy 1–3 weeks later, which may suppurate. It usually resolves in weeks to months; azithromycin shortens it. Toxoplasmosis from cat faeces gives a non-tender generalised lymphadenopathy with a glandular fever-like illness.

questions.question: A 7-year-old has fever, a purpuric rash that does not blanch and neck stiffness (meningococcal disease). Which measure prevents this disease?
questions.b: Long-term oral penicillin for all children
questions.exp: Meningococcal disease is prevented by conjugate MenC/MenACWY and MenB vaccines. Close contacts of a case need chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin or rifampicin) within 24 hours, whatever their vaccine status. Treat the case immediately with IV ceftriaxone (or IM benzylpenicillin before transfer).

questions.question: A boy has recurrent sinus and lung infections, including pneumonia with Haemophilus influenzae. Where is the immune defect most likely?
questions.exp: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae) point to an antibody (B-cell) defect: XLA, CVID, IgA or IgG subclass deficiency. T-cell defects give viral, fungal and opportunistic infections; neutrophil defects give abscesses and fungi; terminal complement defects give Neisseria.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy has difficulty climbing stairs and rises from the floor by pushing on his thighs. His calves are large and firm. CK is 15,000 U/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin gene, X-linked recessive): boys with delayed walking, proximal weakness, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy and a very high CK. Confirm with dystrophin gene testing. Steroids slow decline; watch the heart and breathing. SMA has a normal or mildly raised CK with fasciculations; dermatomyositis has a rash.

questions.question: A 4-year-old has had a cough for 7 weeks. He was treated for pneumonia with antibiotics and for asthma with salbutamol, but he still has a wet cough. What should be suspected?
questions.b: An inhaled foreign body, needing bronchoscopy
questions.c: Asthma needing a higher salbutamol dose
questions.d: Pneumonia needing another 10-day course of antibiotics
questions.exp: A chronic cough (over 4 weeks) that does not respond to treatment needs a cause. In a toddler, an inhaled foreign body can mimic pneumonia (recurrent consolidation in the same lobe) or asthma (wheeze) and needs rigid bronchoscopy. Other causes of chronic wet cough: protracted bacterial bronchitis (2–4 weeks of antibiotics), bronchiectasis, CF, immune deficiency and aspiration.

questions.question: At a party, a child develops sudden wheeze, swollen lips and low blood pressure after eating. What is the first treatment?
questions.exp: Anaphylaxis = allergic skin or mucosal features plus airway, breathing or circulation problems. Give IM adrenaline into the anterolateral thigh (0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL, max 0.5 mg; or 150 micrograms under 6 years, 300 micrograms at 6–12 years), repeat after 5 minutes if needed, with oxygen, fluids and lying flat. Antihistamines and steroids are not first-line.

questions.question: A child has itchy wheals over the body after eating, with no breathing problems, no swelling of the tongue and normal blood pressure. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Urticaria alone, without airway, breathing or circulation compromise, is a mild allergic reaction: give an oral non-sedating antihistamine (cetirizine), observe, and give an allergy plan. Systemic features (stridor, wheeze, hypotension, collapse) mean anaphylaxis and need IM adrenaline.

questions.question: An 8-week-old baby had a brief episode during a feed: she stopped breathing, went floppy and recovered after her mother stimulated her. Examination in the emergency department is completely normal. What should be done?
questions.a: EEG and ECG only, then discharge
questions.e: Admit for observation and further assessment
questions.exp: This is a brief resolved unexplained event (BRUE). Low-risk BRUE needs ALL of: age over 60 days, born at 32 weeks or more, first event, lasting under 1 minute, no CPR by a trained person and a normal examination. Under 60 days of age means a higher-risk BRUE: admit, monitor, and investigate for infection, abuse, cardiac and neurological causes.

questions.question: A 4-month-old had a single brief episode (under 1 minute) of apnoea and floppiness during a feed, and recovered after gentle stimulation. He was born at term, and the examination is completely normal. What should be done?
questions.c: Reassure, educate the parents (including CPR training) and arrange follow-up
questions.e: Start an apnoea monitor at home
questions.exp: This is a low-risk BRUE (over 60 days, term, first event, under 1 minute, no CPR, normal examination). AAP guidance: educate and reassure, offer CPR training, and consider a 12-lead ECG and brief observation; avoid routine bloods, EEG, imaging and home apnoea monitors.

questions.question: A baby born at home has oozing of blood from the umbilical stump. What is the treatment?
questions.exp: Babies born at home often miss the vitamin K injection. Vitamin K deficiency bleeding causes umbilical, gut or skin bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage, with a prolonged PT and normal platelets. Give IV vitamin K (with FFP or prothrombin complex if bleeding is serious).

questions.question: A baby boy bleeds heavily after circumcision. There is no family history of a bleeding disorder, and the platelet count, PT and APTT are all normal. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.exp: Normal PT, APTT and platelets with real bleeding (umbilical stump, circumcision, intracranial) suggests factor XIII deficiency, which stabilises the clot and is not measured by routine tests. Request a specific factor XIII assay or clot solubility test. Haemophilia prolongs the APTT, factor VII deficiency the PT, and vitamin K deficiency the PT.

questions.question: A 14-year-old girl has heavy periods and frequent nosebleeds. Her mother has similar problems. The platelet count is normal and the APTT is slightly prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder (usually autosomal dominant, so girls and boys, with a family history in one parent). It causes mucosal bleeding (nose, gums, heavy periods); the APTT may be prolonged because VWF carries factor VIII. Tests: VWF antigen, VWF activity and factor VIII. Treat with desmopressin (releases stored VWF) or VWF concentrate, and tranexamic acid.

questions.question: An infant has a port-wine stain over the forehead and upper eyelid on one side, and develops focal seizures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sturge–Weber syndrome (somatic GNAQ mutation): facial port-wine stain in the ophthalmic (V1) area, leptomeningeal angioma on the same side (gyral "tram-track" calcification), seizures, hemiparesis, learning problems, and glaucoma. Check eye pressure regularly and image the brain with MRI.

questions.question: A child has puffy eyelids. Urine dipstick shows +++ protein and the urine protein:creatinine ratio is over 200 mg/mmol. What should be checked next?
questions.a: Serum albumin, creatinine and complement C3
questions.exp: The urine already shows nephrotic-range proteinuria. Next confirm the low albumin (under 25 g/L) and check renal function, electrolytes, lipids and C3/C4 (low C3 suggests post-infectious or membranoproliferative disease). A 24-hour urine is no longer needed. Typical steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome (1–12 years, normal BP, C3 and creatinine) is treated with prednisolone without a biopsy.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy has visible blood in the urine 1–2 days after a sore throat. He had a similar episode last year. Blood pressure and complement are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA nephropathy (the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide): recurrent macroscopic haematuria 1–2 days after an upper respiratory infection (synpharyngitic), with normal complement. Post-streptococcal GN comes 1–3 weeks after a throat infection (3–6 weeks after skin), with oedema, hypertension and a LOW C3. Alport syndrome has deafness and a family history.

questions.question: A tall 13-year-old has joint laxity and dislocated lenses (displaced downwards). Marfan syndrome has been excluded. Which test confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, autosomal recessive) looks like Marfan syndrome (tall, long limbs) but has intellectual disability, osteoporosis, thromboembolism and DOWNWARD (inferonasal) lens dislocation; Marfan lenses dislocate UPWARD. Confirm with a high plasma homocysteine and methionine. Treat with pyridoxine (B6) in responders, a low-methionine diet, betaine and folate.

questions.question: A neonate suddenly deteriorates with a very high ammonia and a NORMAL blood gas (no acidosis). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Urea cycle defects (most commonly X-linked OTC deficiency) cause hyperammonaemia with a normal gas or a respiratory alkalosis, never a primary metabolic acidosis. Organic acidaemias (propionic, methylmalonic) also raise ammonia but with a high anion gap metabolic acidosis and ketosis. Stop protein, give IV glucose, ammonia scavengers (sodium benzoate, phenylbutyrate) and arrange dialysis if very high.

questions.question: A child has pinpoint pupils, a blood glucose of 5 mmol/L, a GCS of 8 and a respiratory rate of 10/min. What should be done first?
questions.b: Secure the airway and support breathing (intubation for a GCS of 8)
questions.c: Do a CT head before any treatment
questions.exp: Always start with ABC. A GCS of 8 or less with slow breathing means the airway is not protected and ventilation is failing: support breathing with bag-mask and intubate. Pinpoint pupils with respiratory depression suggest opioid toxicity, so naloxone is also given; organophosphates give pinpoint pupils with secretions and bradycardia (atropine). Flumazenil is avoided in unknown overdoses.

questions.question: A child has been treated for Kawasaki disease. How should he be followed up?
questions.c: Echocardiography at diagnosis, then at 2 weeks and 6–8 weeks
questions.d: No follow-up if the fever settled
questions.exp: Echocardiograms at diagnosis, 1–2 weeks and 4–6 weeks show whether coronary aneurysms develop. Children without aneurysms stop aspirin at 6–8 weeks and need no long-term cardiology follow-up beyond about 1 year; those with aneurysms need long-term follow-up and antiplatelet or anticoagulant treatment depending on size.

questions.question: A stable child has a narrow-complex tachycardia of 260/min. Vagal manoeuvres have not worked. What is the next treatment?
questions.exp: SVT in a stable child: vagal manoeuvres (ice-water to the face in infants, Valsalva in older children), then IV adenosine 100–150 micrograms/kg as a rapid push with a flush via a large vein, increasing to 300 micrograms/kg (max 12 mg). Synchronised cardioversion (1 then 2 J/kg, under sedation) if shocked or adenosine fails. Verapamil is contraindicated in infants.

questions.question: Which virus is most often associated with viral myocarditis in children?
questions.exp: Enteroviruses (coxsackie B, echovirus), adenovirus, parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 are the main causes of viral myocarditis. Cardiac MRI is the standard non-invasive test (myocardial oedema and late gadolinium enhancement); endomyocardial biopsy is the historical gold standard. Treatment is supportive heart failure care; IVIG is sometimes used.

questions.question: After chest trauma, a child is in shock with low blood pressure. The chest X-ray shows a globular heart (pericardial effusion), and he has had a fluid bolus. What should be done next?
questions.b: Transfer to the ward and observe
questions.exp: Cardiac tamponade: shock with muffled heart sounds, raised JVP and pulsus paradoxus after trauma. Fluid helps briefly, but the definitive treatment is draining the pericardium (needle pericardiocentesis, or surgery). Confirm quickly with bedside ultrasound. Diuretics and vasodilators make it worse.

questions.question: A girl developed normally until 12 months, then lost purposeful hand use and speech. She now makes repetitive hand-wringing movements, and her head growth has slowed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Rett syndrome (MECP2, X-linked dominant, almost only girls): normal early development, then regression at 6–18 months with loss of hand skills and speech, hand-wringing or washing movements, acquired microcephaly, breathing irregularities, seizures, scoliosis and gait problems.

questions.question: A girl has the typical regression and hand-wringing of Rett syndrome. Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Rett syndrome is confirmed by finding a MECP2 mutation (about 95% of classical cases). CDKL5 and FOXG1 cause atypical forms. EEG and MRI are often abnormal but not diagnostic, and the karyotype is normal.

questions.question: A mother with sickle cell disease was given morphine for 2 weeks before delivery for painful crises. Two days after birth the baby develops irritability, a high-pitched cry, poor feeding and a seizure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Babies exposed to opioids before birth can develop withdrawal within 1–3 days (later with methadone or buprenorphine): irritability, tremor, high-pitched cry, poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhoea, sweating and sometimes seizures. Score with Finnegan; first comfort care, then oral morphine if severe. Exclude sepsis, glucose and calcium problems. Newborns do not have sickle crises (protected by HbF).

questions.question: Which of these is recommended for a healthy lifestyle in a school-age child?
questions.a: Limit recreational screen time (TV) to no more than about 2 hours a day
questions.b: At least 4 hours of screen time a day for learning
questions.c: Fruit juice instead of water with every meal
questions.d: A television in the bedroom to help sleep
questions.e: 20 minutes of physical activity a week
questions.exp: Health promotion advice: at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity daily, recreational screen time limited (about 2 hours a day or less, none in the hour before bed, no TV in the bedroom), water or milk instead of sugary drinks, regular meals, and enough sleep (9–12 hours at 6–12 years).

questions.question: A 5-week-old boy has projectile non-bilious vomiting after every feed and is hungry after vomiting. Blood tests show low chloride, low potassium and a metabolic alkalosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (2–8 weeks, more in first-born boys): projectile non-bilious vomiting, a hungry baby, an olive-like mass after a test feed, and hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Confirm by ultrasound. Correct fluids and electrolytes first, then do a pyloromyotomy. Salt-wasting CAH gives HIGH potassium and acidosis.

questions.question: A mother is HBsAg positive. What should be given to her newborn?
questions.a: Nothing until the baby is tested at 6 months
questions.c: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin and hepatitis B vaccine within 12 hours of birth, then vaccine at 2, 4 and 6 months
questions.d: Stop breastfeeding and give vaccine at 1 year
questions.e: Hepatitis B vaccine only at 6 months
questions.exp: Babies of HBsAg-positive mothers get HBIG and the first vaccine dose (different sites) within 12 hours, then complete the vaccine series (in the Gulf schedule with the hexavalent vaccine at 2, 4 and 6 months), and are tested for HBsAg and anti-HBs at 9–12 months. This prevents over 90% of transmission. Breastfeeding is allowed.

questions.question: A child with acute pancreatitis still has severe pain despite paracetamol and tramadol. What should be given?
questions.a: Increase the tramadol dose above the maximum
questions.b: No more analgesia, to avoid masking signs
questions.exp: Pain in pancreatitis is severe and needs a strong opioid when step 2 fails: IV morphine (for example 0.1 mg/kg, or as a PCA) with monitoring of sedation and breathing. Good pain control does not hide diagnosis. Codeine is not recommended in children.

questions.question: A teenager has exudative tonsillitis, cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Which test supports the diagnosis?
questions.e: Throat swab for group A streptococcus only
questions.exp: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV): fever, exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, atypical lymphocytes and raised liver enzymes. The Monospot test is positive in most teenagers (often negative under 4 years, when EBV VCA IgM is used). Avoid contact sports for at least 3–4 weeks (splenic rupture), and amoxicillin causes a rash.

questions.question: A child had normal early development, then started losing skills at 9 months and had no words at 18 months. What should be done first?
questions.a: Diagnose autism and start behaviour therapy
questions.c: Start speech therapy without any assessment
questions.exp: Any child with language delay or regression needs a formal audiology test first (and vision), because hearing loss is common and treatable. Regression always needs further work-up: developmental assessment, autism assessment, EEG if seizures or regression in language (Landau–Kleffner), genetic tests (Rett in girls, fragile X) and metabolic screening.

questions.question: The father of a 3-year-old goes hunting and keeps a gun at home. What safety advice should be given?
questions.a: Teach the child not to touch guns; no other measures are needed
questions.b: Store the gun unloaded and locked, with the ammunition locked away separately
questions.c: Store the gun and bullets together in a closed box
questions.d: Keep the gun loaded in a high cupboard
questions.e: Use blank cartridges at home only
questions.exp: Firearm injury prevention: the safest home has no gun. If there is one, store it unloaded and locked (gun safe or trigger lock), with ammunition locked separately, and keys out of children's reach. Young children cannot be relied on to obey "don't touch" rules.

questions.question: A teenage athlete has protein (++) on a urine dipstick at a sports medical. He is well with normal blood pressure. What should be done?
questions.d: Test a first-morning urine sample for protein
questions.exp: Orthostatic (postural) proteinuria is common in tall adolescents: protein appears in the upright position but the first-morning sample (after lying flat overnight) is negative. A negative early-morning protein:creatinine ratio confirms it, and it is benign. If the morning sample is positive, investigate further (UPCR, renal function, BP, complement, ultrasound).

questions.question: A 4-month-old has recurrent kidney stones. Urine shows cystine crystals and raised cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine. What is the management?
questions.c: No treatment until the stones block the kidney
questions.e: High fluid intake and urine alkalinisation, adding a thiol drug (tiopronin) if needed
questions.exp: Cystinuria (autosomal recessive, defect in the renal transporter for cystine, ornithine, lysine and arginine, "COLA") causes recurrent radiolucent-to-faint cystine stones with hexagonal crystals. Treat with a large fluid intake, alkalinising the urine (potassium citrate, pH above 7), lower salt, and tiopronin or penicillamine if stones persist. Cysteamine is for CYSTINOSIS, a different lysosomal disease with Fanconi syndrome and corneal crystals.

questions.question: A boy has hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain and an X-ray showing widening of the lower femur (Erlenmeyer flask deformity). Gaucher disease is diagnosed. What is the management?
questions.c: Bone marrow transplant as first choice
questions.exp: Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase deficiency, autosomal recessive; Gaucher cells with a "crumpled tissue paper" look) causes hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, bone crises and Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the femur. Type 1 (no brain involvement) is treated with enzyme replacement (imiglucerase) or substrate reduction (eliglustat). Splenectomy is avoided.

questions.question: A preterm baby develops abdominal distension and absent bowel sounds. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: In a preterm baby, feed intolerance, abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds and bloody stools mean NEC until proven otherwise. The X-ray shows dilated loops, pneumatosis intestinalis or portal venous gas, and free air with perforation. Stop feeds, decompress with a gastric tube, give IV antibiotics and parenteral nutrition, and involve surgeons.

questions.question: A 9-month-old who is not yet walking has a spiral fracture of the femur. The parents say he fell off the sofa. What is the most important concern?
questions.a: Osteogenesis imperfecta is the only likely cause
questions.exp: A spiral fracture of a long bone in a non-ambulant infant is highly suspicious of abuse (twisting force), especially when the history does not explain it. Start safeguarding: skeletal survey, CT head and eye exam in infants, bone profile and vitamin D, and refer to child protection. A toddler's fracture is a spiral tibial fracture in a child who walks.

questions.question: A child with thyrotoxicosis started carbimazole 2 weeks ago and now has a mild itchy rash, with no fever or sore throat. What should be done?
questions.c: Stop all treatment and give radioactive iodine
questions.d: Continue carbimazole and give an antihistamine
questions.e: Stop carbimazole and switch to propylthiouracil
questions.exp: A mild rash is the most common side effect of carbimazole and often settles with an antihistamine while continuing treatment. Switch drugs if the rash is severe or persists. Propylthiouracil is avoided in children (risk of liver failure). Warn families about agranulocytosis: stop the drug and check a full blood count urgently if there is sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers.

questions.question: A 3-month-old has a first urinary tract infection with E. coli and responds well to antibiotics. What should be done?
questions.exp: Under 6 months, even a typical UTI needs a renal and bladder ultrasound (within 6 weeks; during the illness if atypical). MCUG and DMSA are for atypical or recurrent infections, or abnormal ultrasound. Repeated urine cultures in a well child are not needed.

questions.question: A girl with anorexia nervosa starts refeeding and develops refeeding syndrome. Which hormone drives the complications?
questions.exp: After starvation, carbohydrate intake triggers insulin release. Insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells and causes sodium and water retention, leading to hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, fluid overload and heart failure. Start feeding cautiously, supplement phosphate and thiamine, and monitor electrolytes daily.

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy is referred by his school with depression. He sees violence at home, does not feel safe with his caregiver, and has no access to good nutrition or health care. What further information is most important?
questions.c: A full family and social history, including safety at home and family psychiatric illness
questions.exp: Depression in a child exposed to domestic violence, neglect and lack of care raises safeguarding concerns. The key next information is about the home: who lives there, what violence he sees, whether he is safe, the caregivers' mental health and substance use, and family psychiatric history. Assess risk of self-harm and refer to child protection and mental health services.

questions.question: A child had kernicterus as a newborn. Which type of cerebral palsy is most likely?
questions.exp: Bilirubin damages the basal ganglia (globus pallidus) and brainstem nuclei, causing chronic bilirubin encephalopathy: dyskinetic/athetoid CP, sensorineural hearing loss (auditory neuropathy), upward gaze palsy and dental enamel defects. Spastic diplegia is typical of periventricular leukomalacia in preterm babies.

questions.question: A neonate has a total bilirubin of 200 micromol/L (direct 7). Despite double phototherapy, it rises to 270 micromol/L (direct 6). What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: The rise is unconjugated (the direct fraction is small and not rising), and it rises despite intensive phototherapy, which suggests ongoing haemolysis: ABO or rhesus incompatibility (check blood groups and direct Coombs test) or G6PD deficiency. Biliary atresia and choledochal cyst cause CONJUGATED jaundice (direct over 20% or over 25 micromol/L) with pale stools.
